  • President Trump has announced a landmark diesel deal with Russia aimed at bringing down energy prices. Under the deal, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and another 1 million tons thereafter.
  • In our analysis, these diesel quantities are relatively small compared to global diesel consumption and are unlikely to make a significant difference in prices on their own.  
  • Ukraine has been targeting Russian oil refineries.  This has disrupted Russian fuel production, putting additional pressure on diesel supplies.  To change the landscape, President Trump has also announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, under which both countries would stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure.  However, Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement, and Ukraine was willing to comply if Russia did the same.  Ukraine is already accusing Russia of violating the ceasefire by attacking its power plants, including one in Kharkiv.
  • To allow the deal, the Trump administration has temporarily eased U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel.  In our analysis, reversing part of the pressure Washington has been putting on Russia over the Ukraine war could provide Russia with additional revenue to finance the war.  For investors, the important point is that the additional diesel supply could help at the margin, but meaningful relief in energy prices will depend much more on whether attacks on energy infrastructure stop and whether the broader geopolitical risks ease. 
  • Iran backed Houthi rebels in Yemen launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including a devastating strike on Riyadh’s international airport that killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300.  On an ongoing basis, we have been sharing with you how the conflict in Yemen spills over to Saudi Arabia.
  • In our analysis, the risk to oil supplies is significant.  Saudi Arabia is the world’s largest oil exporter, and the Houthis have demonstrated their ability to strike targets deep inside the country, including oil infrastructure.  Houthis have also threatened shipping through the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a major route for oil shipments.  A successful attack on Saudi oil production or export facilities could disrupt millions of barrels of daily supply.  The danger of a wider war disrupting Saudi oil supplies could easily outweigh the benefit of additional Russian diesel. 
  • The semiconductor industry has been working on a new memory technology called 4F², which allows more memory to be packed into the same space on a chip.  Today’s mainstream DRAM technology uses a 6F² design.  Moving from 6F² to 4F² reduces the area required for each memory cell by one third, potentially increasing memory density by as much as 50% and reducing manufacturing costs.
  • China’s ChangXin Memory Technologies says it has made significant progress with 4F² technology and plans to introduce a product before year end.  The three largest manufacturers Samsung Electronics Co Ltd (OTC:SSNLF), SK Hynix Inc – ADR (NASDAQ:SKHY), and Micron Technology Inc (NASDAQ:MU) are also working on 4F².  In our analysis, the concern for Micron investors is that China’s ChangXin could become a more formidable competitor, leading to increased memory supply and pressure on prices and profit margins.  However, the big question is whether ChangXin can manufacture the 4F² chips in large volumes with acceptable yields, reliability and competitive costs.  As full disclosure, we are long MU from an average of $21.77. 
  • Tomorrow morning will bring earnings from major banks JPMorgan Chase & Co (JPM), Citigroup Inc. (C), The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. (GS), and Wells Fargo & Company (WFC).  As full disclosure, JPM Is in our portfolio, long from an average of $34.14.  C is also in our portfolio.

news.content:
Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and OpenAI are rolling out AI agents, but Americans may adopt them more slowly than consumers in China for a counterintuitive reason: existing services in the West already work pretty well.

Howard Yu, LEGO Professor of Management and Innovation at IMD Business School, told Benzinga the West’s biggest obstacle may be its own convenience.

"Unless it’s perfect, I’m not going to try the alternative. Because life is good," Yu said, describing consumers in Europe and the U.S.

Why China May Move Faster

Yu said one of China’s advantages is the amount of context already sitting inside platforms such as WeChat.

During a visit to Tencent Holdings Ltd. (OTC:TCEHY), Yu saw a WeChat-based agent scan medicine packaging and produce personalized guidance within seconds using information already in the platform. He said that context can make an agent useful without requiring the most advanced model.

Yu said parts of Southeast Asia are on a similar path. In countries such as Indonesia and Vietnam, information has historically been more scattered and coordination more difficult, giving consumers more reason to try new digital services. "Anything better is infinitely better," he said.

Worldpay’s 2026 Agentic Commerce Report found a stark adoption gap: 86% of Chinese consumers were willing to shop with an AI agent, compared with just 45% in the U.S.

Muse Shows Interest, Not Yet Trust

Meta’s Muse suggests Americans are eager to try AI agents. The app reached roughly 2.5 million U.S. downloads through Sept. 19, with its first 12 days on iOS slightly outpacing ChatGPT’s comparable launch.

OpenAI followed with Dots, persistent agents that can carry out longer-running tasks using their own cloud computers and connections to more than 4,000 apps.

But downloading an agent is different from trusting it to make a purchase or booking. Asked whether Muse and Dots had changed his view, Yu said adoption would move at "very, very different" speeds across regions.

Yu cited travel-industry research showing consumers in Asia and the Middle East were much more willing than those in the U.S. and Europe to let an agent book a trip end to end.

Yu called that divergence "not good news" for the U.S., which he described as moving toward "more and more of a fortress economy" as other regions move faster.

US Labs Still Favored to Lead

Prediction market traders expect U.S. labs to dominate the frontier-model race. On Polymarket, Google and Anthropic are nearly tied to have the best AI model at the end of 2026, at about 43% and 42%, respectively. OpenAI follows at roughly 9%, while Meta sits near 3%. The market has attracted about $2.4 million in volume.

Chinese labs remain far behind in the market. Alibaba is around 1%, while DeepSeek, ByteDance and other Chinese names trade below 1%.

But the market measures model performance, not adoption. Yu’s argument is that China could move faster on AI agents even as U.S. companies continue to build the most capable models.

SambaNova Systems, a privately held artificial intelligence chip startup, has seen its indicative share price surge more than threefold over the past year, dramatically outpacing NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) as investors look for alternatives to the dominant supplier of AI computing hardware.

SambaNova’s Forge Price reached $70.13 per share on Oct. 12, up 259.27% over one year, according to Forge Global. That puts its indicative share price at roughly 3.6 times its level a year earlier.

By comparison, NVIDIA delivered a 23.73% one-year total return as of Oct. 12, including dividends and other distributions, according to data from Perplexity Finance. SambaNova’s percentage gain was more than 10 times NVIDIA’s return over the period.

The comparison comes as investors pour money into the computing infrastructure needed to train and run increasingly capable AI models.

Read Also: SoftBank Wants up to $100 Billion From Gulf Investors for AI — but Its $65 Billion OpenAI Bet Is Raising Eyebrows

Competing for AI Compute

SambaNova and NVIDIA compete in AI computing, particularly in the market for hardware used to run AI models, known as inference. However, the companies have different approaches to the market.

NVIDIA dominates the AI accelerator market with its graphics processing units, networking equipment and software ecosystem. SambaNova is developing specialized chips called reconfigurable dataflow units, or RDUs, designed to handle demanding AI workloads, including inference for large language models.

The companies’ technologies can also complement each other. In June, SambaNova demonstrated a system that used NVIDIA’s B200 GPUs to process incoming prompts and SambaNova’s SN40 chips to generate responses. The company said the combined architecture delivered twice the inference speed of a B200-only configuration, according to SambaNova.

Private-Market Pricing Surges

Forge’s latest data puts SambaNova’s implied valuation at approximately $6.07 billion. That is below the $11 billion post-money valuation reported for the company’s Series F financing in July, when SambaNova announced a funding round that included an initial close of more than $800 million, according to Forge’s funding history and TechCrunch.

The gap highlights an important distinction between private-market pricing and formal fundraising valuations. Forge Price is a derived estimate based on private-market data, not a continuously traded stock quote or a guarantee of the price investors can obtain in a transaction.

SambaNova’s share-price rally nevertheless points to investor interest in alternatives to conventional GPU-based AI infrastructure as inference workloads grow.

NVIDIA remains a vastly larger business, with a market capitalization of approximately $5.45 trillion as of Sept. 23, according to a report from the Motley Fool.

As demand for AI computing continues to grow, SambaNova’s rally highlights investor interest in alternatives to NVIDIA’s dominant GPU platform. Whether that momentum translates into lasting gains will depend on the company’s ability to turn demand for its specialized chips into broader adoption and commercial growth.

Many investors know that the S&P 500 is heavily weighted to companies with exposure to the artificial intelligence sector. Data shows that the market capitalization of AI pure plays in the index is now reaching record levels last seen in the 19th century.

AI Dominance in the S&P 500

AI stocks make up 49% of the S&P 500, which is tracked by the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), which could explain some of the fears of an AI bubble popping.

Data from Bianco Research shared on social media shows that along with making up 49% of the S&P 500, the 41 companies named as AI pure plays in the index make up around two-thirds of the S&P 500’s year-to-date market cap changes.

Bianco Research’s Jim Bianco takes things a step further, with just how concentrated in AI the S&P 500 could be had rules been changed or could become in the future.

"If SpaceX was in the $SPX now, AI-related stocks would be 51% of the index. With Anthropic and OpenAI coming public, add them to the $SPX in 2027 and AI would be ~55% of the $SPX," Bianco tweeted.

The S&P 500 declined to change its rules to include SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) stock early, instead holding to the normal principles that a company needs profitability and has sufficient float.

Bianco shares that the precedent of AI stocks making up this much of the U.S. stock market dates back more than 100 years.

"The last time a single theme was >50% of the $SPX was the railroads in the 19th century."

Bianco shared the list of AI pure plays in the S&P 500, which includes all of the top 10 holdings in the SPY:

  • NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA)
  • Apple Inc (NASDAQ:AAPL)
  • Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT)
  • Amazon.com Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN)
  • Alphabet Inc Class A (NASDAQ:GOOGL)
  • Broadcom Inc (NASDAQ:AVGO)
  • Alphabet Class C (NASDAQ:GOOG)
  • Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META)
  • Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU)
  • Tesla Inc (NASDAQ:TSLA)

While all the Magnificent Seven stocks are included in the index, the list also includes AI utilities, AI capital equipment companies and a list of AI direct companies across software, cybersecurity and other technology fields.

Read Also: EXCLUSIVE: Top 12 Most-Searched Tickers in September on Benzinga Pro – Meta Rises, SpaceX Falls, Dell & Bloom Energy Join List

Going Back to the Railroads

The S&P 500 was launched in 1957, so it hasn’t been around long enough to be dominated by the railroad sector.

The 1880s did see the overall U.S. stock market capitalization dominated by the sector, which emerged as the top sector and dominated the country.

In 1881, railroad companies made up 63% of U.S. stock market capitalization, according to Bank of America data.

Today, railroads make up less than 1%. The railroad sector has been a strong performer, though, beating the overall U.S. stock market since 1900.

A newsletter from BeBusiness Smart notes that sectors have dominated the S&P 500 or the overall U.S. stock market index at other times, but never near the 63% seen from the late 1880s to 1900. Here were some standout time periods of sector dominance:

  • Railroad, 1900: 63%
  • Energy, 1980: 28%
  • Technology, March 1980: 33% to 35%
  • Financials, before 2008: 20% to 22%
  • Technology, October 2026: 40%+

Railroads led to one of the greatest expansions of the U.S. economy, lowering freight and transportation costs and connecting many areas across the country.

AI is viewed as a technology that could change and impact multiple sectors in similar ways. The question is whether AI representing more than 50% of the U.S. stock market would be good or raise even more questions about a potential bubble.

Navitas Semiconductor Corp (NASDAQ:NVTS) shares are moving higher in Monday’s after-hours session after the company announced its latest power delivery board, developed in collaboration with Nvidia.

  • Navitas Semiconductor stock is trending. What’s driving NVTS stock?

Navitas Unveils 800 V-to-12 V Power Delivery Board 

Navitas on Monday announced its latest 24 kW, 800 V-to-12 V DC-DC power delivery board, powered by GaNFast technology and developed in collaboration with NVIDIA Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA). The system is designed to support the Nvidia MGX ecosystem and advance 800 VDC power architectures for AI data centers.

The single-stage architecture converts 800 VDC directly to 12 VDC and can deliver 24 kW to power a full compute tray, with a target efficiency of 97% at full load. The board mounts directly on the compute motherboard, close to the xPUs, which cuts losses along the power path and supports high power demands.

“The next era of AI will be defined not only by how much compute we can create but by our ability to deliver the power needed to unleash its full potential,” said Chris Allexandre, president and CEO of Navitas. “Our collaboration with Nvidia is breaking the AI infrastructure power wall by reimagining power delivery from 800 VDC to the GPU.”

NVTS Shares Jump After Hours

Navitas shares were up 6.21% in after-hours on Monday, trading at $10.61 at the time of publication, according to Benzinga Pro.

President Donald Trump’s administration is reportedly planning to move three senior officials from the Commerce Department’s Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) to the White House, after coordination problems with the department.

Coordination Problems Behind CAISSI Shift

The three officials, whose names have not been disclosed, would report to Michael Kratsios, director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy, and National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, according to a Reuters report, citing The Information.

A White House official told The Information that coordination problems with the Commerce Department showed the need to bring CAISSI’s leadership closer to the White House’s artificial intelligence decision-making process.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick invited Kratsios and Cairncross to co-manage the center six months ago, according to a senior Commerce official.

The White House and the Commerce Department did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comment.

Read Also: Stock Market: Will S&P 500 Open Up or Down Today?

White House Consolidates AI Oversight

Earlier this month, Trump named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton the administration’s AI czar, tasking him with coordinating federal efforts to maintain U.S. leadership in the technology.

Last week, Trump said that the White House considers anyone who uses the term ‘artificial intelligence’ instead of ‘super intelligence’ an “enemy.”

CAISSI Anchors Frontier AI Testing

CAISSI evaluates advanced AI models for safety and capabilities and plays a role in the administration’s framework for testing frontier AI systems before they are deployed.

Last month, Trump released the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, a voluntary safety pact signed by the executives of leading AI companies, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) xAI, Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL), and Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), that calls for independent audits, stronger internal controls, and board-level oversight of frontier AI models.

Over the past four years, market volatility has given investors several reasons to exit their positions. However, CNBC’s Jim Cramer said those who stayed invested instead of selling have benefited from their patience.

Cramer Backs Staying Invested for the Long Term

The S&P 500 has climbed about 118% since hitting a low on Oct. 12, 2022, despite facing many challenges, including steep Federal Reserve interest-rate increases, a banking-sector crisis, broad tariff measures and the Iran war. The rally took shape when concerns over inflation and economic growth weighed heavily on sentiment, but these headwinds have failed to reverse the market’s upward trajectory, CNBC reported.

“No matter what the most important point is that the consistent invested. Putting money in work regularly, including Bad times in stocks and indices, is by far the best strategy towards wealth,” said Cramer on the show Mad Money.

Cramer noted that $10,000 invested in the S&P 500 when it reached its October 2022 low would have grown to nearly $23,061 currently. He also highlighted that several major tech stocks posted substantially stronger gains during the same period. Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) shares jumped about 1,875%, lifting a $10,000 investment to around $197,505, while Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ: META) surged 488%, increasing the same initial investment to more than $58,800. Both companies are held in Cramer’s Charitable Trust portfolio managed by CNBC’s Investing Club, the report added.

“We could not have predicted even the big declines or the big rebounds,” said Cramer. “The bottom line, stay in, keep buying, don’t lose faith. Those are the lessons from this indomitable and intrepid four-year-old bull market.”

On Monday, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE: SPY) and Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (NASDAQ: QQQ), which track the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100, respectively, closed mixed. SPY fell 0.06% to $778.10, while QQQ declined 0.70% to $746.04. Meanwhile, the Dow tracker, State Street SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (NYSE: DIA), ended 0.35% higher at $517.91.

Nvidia closed down 1.29% to $226.32 on Monday, while Meta rose 3.38% to $742.96. Year-to-date, Nvidia has soared around 21.35%, while Meta has surged about +12.55%.

Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the company was prepared to write a $100 billion to $200 billion check for its AI ambitions.

During a recent podcast appearance, Zuckerberg detailed the financial commitments and strategic rationale behind Meta Superintelligence Labs and its new AI model, Muse Wonder.

Massive Infrastructure Investment

Zuckerberg recounted executive discussions from late last year regarding the scale of the company’s capital expenditure. He told Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang, “we’re going to write this check for, like, I don’t know, like $100 billion, $200 billion,” before asking, “Alex, are you sure this is going to work?”

To support its AI ambitions, Zuckerberg explained that Meta is constructing high-capacity computing facilities. This includes a “Prometheus” cluster in Ohio scaling beyond one gigawatt and a planned “Hyperion” cluster in Louisiana that will scale to five gigawatts.

Zuckerberg estimated that operating a single gigawatt cluster costs approximately $15 billion annually, while the upfront capital expenditures for such a facility can reach $50 billion to $60 billion.

Read Also: Jim Cramer Calls Mark Zuckerberg's Meta a ‘Monster Long’ as Muse AI Retention Proves ‘Almost as Good as ChatGPT’

Strategic Positioning and Returns

When asked about the financial risk of these unprecedented investments, Zuckerberg defended the strategy. He stated that the company’s highly profitable core business and strong credit allow Meta to underwrite the costs.

This infrastructure buildout, Zuckerberg said, will “position the company to really lead in the area for decades to come.”

Zuckerberg also noted that the financial risk is mitigated by broader industry demand for computing power. He stated that if Meta’s specific AI consumer products fail, but AI technology succeeds broadly, other technology companies will be willing to pay to use Meta’s computing capacity.

Business and Consumer AI Agents

Zuckerberg emphasized that Meta aims to build personal superintelligence focused on “invention and creation,” rather than strictly automating knowledge work.

The company plans to monetize its Muse AI models through premium consumer subscriptions and by offering AI tools that function as a “business in a box” for small enterprises, according to Zuckerberg.

Ultimately, Zuckerberg stated, these revenue streams and the acceleration of Meta’s core business will make the AI products self-funding.

How Has META Performed in 2026?

(NASDAQ:AAPL) can keep selling iPhones by the million and still lose the artificial intelligence game, according to investor Gene Munster, who warned that Siri could be shut out of the money if users settle into Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse or Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s (NASDAQ:SPCX) Grokbot first.

Users Will Be Hard to Win Back

In a post on X, the Managing Partner at Deepwater Asset Management said that once people connect their lives to an AI, set up their workflows, and start paying $20 or more a month, it will be harder to get them to switch to Siri in any meaningful way.

“Siri can be a great personal AI, but Apple needs to move faster,” Munster added.

A Window for Apple

On the Fathom podcast episode with Munster, fellow managing partner Doug Clinton said the bigger risk is to the upside case for Siri rather than to the device ecosystem, adding that Apple probably needs “more urgency” because “there is a window here.”

Once people get locked into rival assistants, he said, they will be “hard to convert.”

Muse Pulls Ahead on Agent Features

Meta launched Muse last month as an agent that opens a browser, fills in forms, and keeps working after the app is closed, and it passed 2.5 million downloads in its first two weeks.

Bank of America Securities analyst Wamsi Mohan said Apple can keep every handset sale and still lose discovery, referral and transaction initiation.

Apple shipped a rebuilt Siri AI with iOS 27 last month, built on custom Google Gemini models, but Mohan said it still lacks persistent background tasks, third-party action coverage, and a payment rail at Muse’s level.

However, Yorkville Ives’ Dan Ives argued in a note last week that Apple does not need the best AI model, because its more than 2.5 billion active devices make it “the toll collector on the consumer AI highway.”

The banking sector has diverged from the broader equity rally. While the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:SPY) is up about 14% for the year, the five largest U.S. banks, measured by the Invesco KBW Bank ETF (NASDAQ:KBWB), have collectively dipped around $270 billion from summer peaks.

Institutional investors have retreated – with only 35% expecting banks to beat the broader market, the Truist Securities survey showed, according to BigGo Finance. Compared with about 82% in December 2025, the decline reflects the repricing of bond yields.

Earnings season starts today, with JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE:JPM), Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (NYSE:GS), Wells Fargo & Co. (NYSE:WFC), and Citigroup Inc. (NYSE:C) reporting before the market opens.

The Yield Shock

Net interest margin is the gap between what banks earn on their assets and what they pay to fund them. That margin is now under pressure. Since the Fed raised its benchmark rate in September, deposit and wholesale funding costs have climbed as lenders fight to hold on to cash.

“Loan growth is easier to find than deposit growth, and so it’s putting pressure on deposit dynamics of raising funds,” said Brendan Coughlin, president of Citizens Financial Group.

The 10-year Treasury yield is trading around 5.24%, and the 30-year around 5.55%. Higher rates make borrowing harder for corporate clients and increase the risk of trouble with floating-rate debt and commercial real estate loans coming up for renewal.

Not everyone sees a squeeze coming. “Banks are asset-sensitive still,”  Matt Stucky, chief portfolio manager for equities at Northwestern Mutual, said according to MarketWatch.

Stucky notes that bank loans reprice faster than deposits. FactSet consensus shows net interest income rising across several big lenders, led by JPMorgan Chase, which is projected to grow 5.4% from the prior quarter and 12.2% from a year earlier.

See More: Top Value Stocks

The Dealmaking Drag

After a blockbuster second quarter, profit expectations have been subdued. Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s (NASDAQ:SPCX) record $85 billion IPO in June boosted that quarter.

Since then, high financing costs have slowed merger announcements. NVIDIA-backed Firmus Grid shelved its listing this week after investors pushed back on its valuation.

“A great deal of the recent underperformance for banks has been driven by the dramatic rise in long-term rates,” UBS analyst Erika Najarian told clients. Deutsche Bank research puts the specially serviced rate on securitized commercial real estate loans at 12%.

Others think the selloff has gone too far. Chris Grisanti of MAI Capital Management called the pullback “more of an opportunity than a harbinger of a downturn.” RBC Capital Markets‘ Gerard Cassidy said “underlying fundamentals remain strong” and the economy is “nowhere near a recession.”

“The No. 1 credit input is unemployment, which has been under 5% for 61 consecutive quarters,” said Macrae Sykes, portfolio manager of the actively-managed Gabelli Financial Services Opportunities ETF (NYSE:GABF).

Citigroup’s global co-head of M&A Guillermo Baygual sees demand holding up. 

“Yes, the interest rate environment is not helpful, but as a topic in the boardroom, M&A hasn’t slowed down,” he said.

Alexandr Wang, Chief AI Officer at Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), has been taking notes on Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) CEO Elon Musk, and one lesson made it all the way to Mark Zuckerberg and into the center of the company’s artificial intelligence strategy.

Small Teams, Fast Moves

In a podcast appearance with David Senra published on Monday, Wang said Musk has demonstrated at various points in his career that a “small, incredibly cracked, highly technical team” that is very flat can get a great deal done.

“You can accomplish a lot very, very quickly,” Wang said.

Wang added that the approach was something he discussed with Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg early in his time at Meta.

Zuckerberg was excited about it, according to Wang, and it became one of the “tentpoles” of Meta’s strategy, built on a flat, highly technical team with “very high talent density.”

Read Also: Gene Munster Warns Apple Can Sell Millions of iPhones and Still Lose the AI Game as Users Could Lock Into Muse and Grok

Meta Cut Workforce to Bet Bigger on AI

In May, Meta cut about 10% of its global workforce and reassigned roughly 7,000 employees to AI-focused teams in a restructuring designed to support its growing investments in the technology.

However, Zuckerberg reportedly told employees that the reorganization did not unfold as “clean” as planned, according to Reuters.

Speed Beats Headcount

Influencer Mario Nawfal said on X that Meta is “now deliberately borrowing from the way Elon builds small, highly technical teams.”

He added that “at some point, adding more people stops making you faster,” and that in AI, “the speed of a decision can matter as much as the resources behind it.”

When Musk took over Twitter, now X, in 2022, he slashed its global workforce by thousands.

Musk’s Lean Teams

Andrej Karpathy, a former AI director at Tesla Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA), said in 2024 that Musk “was always like a force against growth.”

He said Musk’s approach minimizes middle management and favors technical expertise over hierarchy, treating engineers as “the source of truth.”

Box Inc. (NYSE:BOX) CEO Aaron Levie said AI agent swarms could become a major part of enterprise workflows, with cybersecurity emerging as a key application as businesses look to identify vulnerabilities across increasingly complex systems.

AI Agent Swarms Could Reshape Enterprise Cybersecurity

On Monday, in a post on X, Levie said agent swarms would become integral to enterprise operations because they could use computing power to tackle problems that can be broken into multiple tasks and handled simultaneously.

"Agent swarms are going to be a core part of many enterprise workflows in the future," Levie wrote.

He identified cybersecurity as one of the biggest potential beneficiaries, highlighting the ability of AI agents to test numerous possible attack scenarios without fatigue.

"Cyber will be one of the biggest beneficiaries of this," he said, pointing to the broad range of potential vulnerabilities and the need to chain together different scenarios to achieve an exploit.

AI Cybersecurity Could Drive Enterprise Token Demand

Levie also noted that large companies must protect a wide range of assets, including IT systems, software, physical infrastructure and data.

"This will become one of the biggest token uses in large enterprises given the range of IT systems, software, physical infrastructure, and data that needs to be protected at all times," he wrote.

He concluded his post by describing the developments as "Super interesting times in cyber."

AI Leaders Sounded Alarm on AI’s Future

Last month, Mark Cuban warned that social media algorithms could amplify anti-AI sentiment even as Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) invested billions in AI, potentially profiting from content that fueled opposition to the technology.

This transition from foundational AI models that process information to autonomous AI agents that can execute complex, multi-step tasks on behalf of users represents the next major phase of industry development.

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) is losing ground in China’s AI chip market, as export restrictions and Beijing’s push for domestic technology strengthen Huawei Technologies’ position.

An IDC report found Nvidia held 34% of China’s AI accelerator market during the first half of 2026, while Huawei’s share reached 28%, narrowing the gap after Nvidia shipped 678,000 accelerators between January and June, Reuters reported. That total represented a 44% decline for Nvidia chips from the same period last year, according to the report.

IDC did not clarify which Nvidia chips accounted for its 34% market share or whether the figure included restricted B200 and B300 chips, which have reportedly been smuggled into China.

Huawei shipped 572,000 accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier. Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. (NYSE:BABA) unit T-Head captured 7%, while Cambricon Technologies Corp. held 5%, the report added.

China’s total accelerator shipments climbed to 2.008 million units. GPU shipments declined 26% to 991,000, while other accelerator shipments increased nearly 80% to 1.016 million.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comments.

Read Also: Tim Cook Meets China’s Vice Premier as Apple Doubles Down on Its Biggest Overseas Market — Beijing Calls for ‘Stable’ US Ties

Huawei Expands Chip And Software Challenge to Nvidia

U.S. restrictions on advanced AI chip exports have limited Nvidia’s available products in China. Beijing has also encouraged domestic alternatives and introduced approval requirements for Nvidia imports that comply with Washington’s rules.

The market shift follows a broader expansion by Huawei. In September, the company introduced more than 10 chipsets spanning AI accelerators, processors and connectivity components, targeting infrastructure dominated by Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) and Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC).

That hardware push is being reinforced by software development. Later that month, DeepSeek partnered with Huawei on open-source software for Ascend chips, challenging Nvidia’s CUDA platform, which has helped maintain developer reliance on its processors.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in May that Huawei was "very, very strong" and acknowledged Nvidia had "largely conceded" the China market as export controls accelerated the domestic chip ecosystem. “I don’t have any expectation,” Huang said.

Shares of Nvidia dipped about 0.90% to $224.29 premarket on Tuesday.

AI’s seemingly insatiable appetite for electricity has brought nuclear energy back to the top of the clean-energy list. Yet even resilient fuel pricing and power agreements involving Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), and Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) haven’t stopped the equity retreat.

Contracts Delay the Payoff

According to Kalkin, Cameco Corp. (NYSE:CCJ), the world’s second-largest uranium producer, had a first-quarter realized uranium price of $65.45 a pound, well below the subsequent futures benchmark.

The disconnect from spot prices reflects the industry reality. Uranium contracts are long-dated, spanning years, and higher prices don’t immediately translate into higher producer revenue like with many other commodities.

Supply constraints nevertheless persist. Delays at Kazatomprom’s TQZ sulphuric acid plant are limiting the leaching process used to extract uranium at its in-situ operations.

“High prices did not really cure high prices,” Independent Speculator’s Lobo Tiggre said in a recent interview, arguing that stronger prices had not unleashed the anticipated supply surge.

Execution and financing risks remain significant. Reactor developer NuScale Power Corporation (NYSE:SMR) has fallen 53% year to date, even though its outlook depends more on reactor deployment than uranium prices.

Tiggre also suggested doubts about returns on artificial-intelligence spending could be weighing on uranium shares, now treated partly as an AI infrastructure trade.

Buying the Disconnect

After building cash through profit-taking in precious-metals equities, Tiggre said he had begun adding to uranium holdings.

“Right now, the most compelling speculation I see in the whole commodity sector is the other yellow metal,” he said. “It’s actually uranium.”

His argument centers on spot uranium trading in the low $90s while long-term contracts command prices in the high $90s. He described the lag behind a rising term benchmark as unusually prolonged.

He argued that nine months of disappointing price action matters little against nuclear projects’ multidecade horizons. He also cited an Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) nuclear-power agreement as evidence of strengthening demand.

“When price and value diverge, there’s opportunity,” he said.

Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) is expanding Starlink’s U.S. wireless ambitions through a nationwide spectrum purchase, while analysts weigh the opportunity against the cost and technical challenges of competing with established telecom carriers.

SpaceX agreed to acquire a nationwide low-band wireless spectrum portfolio from Grain Management in a deal reportedly valued at $8 billion.

The stock has risen more than 20% above its IPO price and, according to CNBC host Scott Wapner, ranks as the sixth-largest company in the Nasdaq 100 behind NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL), Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN).

MoffettNathanson Sees Strong Business, but Questions Wireless Economics

MoffettNathanson research analyst Julie Zhu said she views SpaceX’s execution and leadership positively but questioned the market’s reaction to the spectrum deal.

She told CNBC on Monday that Starlink’s satellite-based wireless service still faces major disadvantages against the Big Three (implying AT&T Inc. (NYSE: T), T-Mobile US Inc. (NASDAQ:TMUS) and Verizon Communications Inc. (NYSE:VZ)).

Zhu said the service is “not competitive with the Big Three and what they’re offering,” pointing to weaker signals over long distances and the difficulty of matching terrestrial networks.

She also noted that the three carriers still control roughly 14 to 15 times more spectrum than SpaceX, even after the acquisition.

Building comparable coverage would also take years and significant capital.

See More: Top Value Stocks

Broadband, AI Remain Key Growth Drivers

Zhu said SpaceX still has meaningful value across its broadband business and other growth opportunities.

She also pointed to the company’s AI operations as an important part of its valuation, saying Grok and xAI will require continued investment.

SpaceX must balance those opportunities against other capital demands, including roughly $100 billion earmarked for Louisiana and Starship development, additional research spending and broader rocket investment.

Zhu said the AI business currently offers a one-year payback, while the potential return from a major wireless buildout remains uncertain.

MoffettNathanson maintains a $142 price forecast on SpaceX.

The analyst’s valuation reflects concerns that investor expectations may be running ahead of the economic returns SpaceX can generate from its wireless ambitions.

Isaacson Sees a Much Larger Opportunity

Perella Weinberg advisory partner and Tulane University professor Walter Isaacson took a more optimistic view of the wireless opportunity.

“He bid on it, he got the 800 MHz spectrum,” Isaacson told CNBC. “This is huge,” Isaacson said, pointing to Musk’s view that the potential market could approach the size of the global economy.

Bernstein Sees Opportunity for Tower Operators

Bernstein analyst Madison Rezaei said SpaceX could become a fourth major customer for U.S. tower companies.

“What we suddenly have is a new carrier on the tower companies,” Rezaei said. She estimated that another tenant could lift recurring tower revenue by roughly 10%-15%.

Rezaei also said SpaceX is more likely to partner with an existing wireless carrier than build an entirely new tower network, while Zhu questioned whether such a roaming agreement would ultimately materialize.

  • Its new Cue personal agent competes directly with Meta’s Muse, while major Chinese tech companies are pursuing similar customers

Manus once looked set to build its future as an agentic AI operator helping users perform everyday tasks like booking tickets and ordering products online from inside the Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) universe. Now, the Chinese-founded startup, freshly divorced from Meta, has raised more than $500 million to pursue that future independently, while its former buyer competes for the same business.

Manus parent Butterfly Effect announced the financing on Oct. 8, naming Boyu Capital and IDG Capital as co-leaders of the round. Existing big-name investors including Tencent (0700.HK), HSG and ZhenFund also participated.

The money gives Manus new ammunition to turn its early success with AI agents into a lasting business. These applications carry out research and other computer tasks for users, going beyond simply answering questions. Manus helped popularize that promise when it made its public debut in March 2025. But as more larger companies offer similar capabilities, Manus’ early-mover status is becoming less important.

Its return to independence followed an unusual round trip. Meta announced its acquisition of Manus in December 2025, in what was seen as a major validation for China’s efforts to make AI more practical and commercial. But then China’s national economic planner took the unusual step of ordering the deal unwound on April 27, and Manus formally resumed independent operations on Sept. 1.

Its founders and earlier investors helped buy the company back from Meta at a reported $2 billion valuation. Bloomberg reported in September that Manus was seeking a $4 billion valuation for its next financing, twice the buyback figure. The company did not disclose the final valuation from its latest funding round.

For those returning investors, the appeal goes back well before the excitement surrounding AI agents. They are backing founders for their experience building practical software and persuading people to pay for it – two relatively rare commodities in the young AI sector.

Top team

Manus Chief executive Xiao Hong started out creating tools for WeChat, helping users edit public-account posts and manage customers in China’s leading social app. He established Butterfly Effect in 2022 and began working on Monica, an AI assistant available through a browser extension.

Chief scientist Ji Yichao brought experience building a mobile browser and working on search. Product partner Zhang Tao had worked on international products at ByteDance before leading product development at AI startup Light Year Beyond. Their backgrounds combined the technical work of building applications with experience selling them.

Some investors followed that development for years. ZhenFund partner Liu Yuan said in June 2025 that his firm had invested five times in Xiao Hong and his team across their ventures since 2016. He also helped introduce Ji to Xiao when the latter was exploring an AI browser.

Manus moved its headquarters and core team to Singapore in 2025 as it expanded overseas. But Xiao and Ji were reportedly prevented from leaving China after regulators summoned them to Beijing in March this year to examine the Meta acquisition.

Despite that, development at the company continued. Xiao, Ji and Zhang coordinated with their Singapore colleagues through daily video calls, and the company continued releasing updates. Meantime, business for the Manus AI agent was exploding, with annual recurring revenue exceeded $300 million during the investigation, according to a LatePost report in August.

Xiao expressed his hopes for a fresh start in a late-September post on Chinese social platform Jike. "I thought our journey would end as a footnote. Perhaps we have a chance to write a chapter," he wrote.

That ambition soon took a more concrete form. On Sept. 28, Manus launched its 2.0 version and Cue, a separate app for personal agents. Cue gives agents their own email addresses, phone numbers and computers so they can handle tasks on a user’s behalf. It puts Manus squarely in competition with Meta’s Muse, launched earlier that month with a similar promise of a personal agent that gets things done.

Life goes on

With the Meta-Manus separation complete, Xiao and Ji’s travel restrictions were reportedly lifted by Oct. 8. Manus was expanding its Beijing team while retaining its Singapore base. A product was being prepared for the tightly controlled China market, where its Manus 2.0 and Cue aren’t available and most of the major global players aren’t active.

Meantime, the competition abroad already extends well beyond Meta. OpenAI’s dots, available through ChatGPT, can research topics, analyze data and prepare documents. Anthropic began merging Cowork and chat into Claude in September, bringing more work into its main assistant, including handling files and operating a user’s computer through its desktop app.

Those capabilities make the case for a separate Manus subscription harder to sustain unless the Chinese company can deliver noticeably better results. At the same time, Manus may also suffer from concerns about data privacy linked to its China roots, similar to TikTok, leading some global users to opt for rival products without such ties.

China offers another market for Manus to pursue, but that market is also quite competitive. Despite its position as a key investor, Tencent also offers its own WorkBuddy in China for office tasks and CodeBuddy for software development. Alibaba (BABA) (9988.HK) offers Qoder coding tools and QoderWork for desktop collaboration, while ByteDance’s Doubao Work also handles research, documents, spreadsheets and data analysis.

Xiao’s response is to keep the company’s ambitions broad. In his Jike post, he compared the business to selling computers: people mainly buy them to work, but also want entertainment and creativity. That gives Manus, which relies on other developers’ underlying AI models, more uses to pursue.

Its new Cascade system offers one example of how it is trying to do that. Manus says the system brings in specialized capabilities only when a task needs them, reducing unnecessary processing and saving computing power. Cascade cost 32% less to run than its previous system in one tested configuration, though that’s a company-reported result.

If Manus can repeat those savings across everyday tasks, it would have more room to improve its margins or offer better prices. Another strong advantage would be completing work reliably enough that customers need to spend less time checking and correcting it.

That operating record will matter if Manus eventually seeks a public listing. Reuters reported that a Hong Kong IPO would not begin until at least 2027, leaving the company time to show what it can achieve independently.

Its returning investors have already backed the founders once, helped buy the company back and supplied fresh money for expansion. Whether their confidence is justified will depend on whether customers believe that Manus still does enough useful work to keep subscribing.

The U.S. government would rescue Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) in a crisis, but might let Google or Meta fail, according to Liz Hoffman, business editor at Semafor.

“I do not think the government would step in to save Meta or Google. I do think they would step in to save Nvidia,” Hoffman said Tuesday on the Prof G Markets podcast.

Hoffman, who covered banks after the 2008 financial crisis, argues Nvidia has become so deeply involved in financing the AI boom that it increasingly resembles AIG, the insurer Washington rescued during the crisis.

Nvidia Becomes the AI Industry’s Banker

Nvidia has become a major investor in the AI boom it supplies, taking stakes in 229 private companies and 13 publicly traded firms across the industry.

Hoffman previously described Nvidia as “both a bank, a financial supporter and a security blanket for the entire industry.”

She compared its financing arrangements to parents “co-signing on your first apartment,” explaining how Nvidia uses its financial strength to support less creditworthy customers.

One example is Nvidia’s agreement in August to provide up to $105 billion in guarantees for an Ohio data-center campus leased to OpenAI.

If OpenAI defaults, Nvidia could have to cover some rent and electricity payments. It has also agreed to protect the site’s value, potentially making up the difference if a new tenant or buyer pays less than a guaranteed minimum.

The campus is expected to use almost exclusively Nvidia equipment, and the company estimates that each generation of hardware installed there could generate $150 billion to $200 billion in revenue.

Why Hoffman Sees Echoes of AIG

AIG nearly collapsed in 2008 after selling billions of dollars in guarantees on mortgage-linked investments. When those investments plunged in value, the insurer faced enormous demands for cash, forcing Washington to step in with an $85 billion rescue.

Hoffman sees a potential parallel: if AI demand disappoints, Nvidia could face weaker chip sales alongside losses on investments and guarantees supporting the same customers.

“A really bad headline would be Nvidia sells its stake in Intel,” she said, describing how selling assets to raise cash could frighten investors.

However, Hoffman emphasized Nvidia’s strong balance sheet, calling its recent $150 billion buyback authorization increase “a flex.”

The IMF warned Tuesday that an AI investment slowdown could destabilize financial markets, according to Reuters.

On Polymarket, traders put the chance of a qualifying AI-industry downturn at just 6% by December 31, rising to 19% by June 2027.

Even if Hoffman is right about a government rescue, AIG’s experience offers Nvidia shareholders a warning: saving the company doesn’t necessarily mean saving investors.
